standard.title: Create geographical descriptions and explanations
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and responses, using geographical knowledge and methods, concepts, terms and reference sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have prior communication skills from F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S07: present descriptions and explanations, drawing ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources, and using relevant terms and conventions). This standard raises the bar specifically for geographical communication — incorporating geographical methods (maps, graphs, data representations), geographical concepts, specialised terminology, and reference to sources as integrated elements of geographical writing and presentation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and responses using geographical knowledge and methods, concepts, terms and reference sources.

nodes.label: Geographical descriptions with concepts and terminology
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create geographical descriptions that use accurate terminology, reference geographical concepts, and connect the audience to the topic.
nodes.minimum_width: Students produce a geographical description that uses at least three accurate geographical terms and references at least one geographical concept.
nodes.typical_width: Students create descriptions that connect the audience to a geographical topic and use geographical concepts and terms accurately — e.g. describing a preferred liveability strategy using terms such as distribution, accessibility, walkability, sustainability, and concepts such as place or interconnections.
wider: Compare a geographical description written for a specialist audience (planners, geographers) with one written for a general community audience — examine how terminology use and concept explanation differ
Evaluate the precision of geographical terminology in a description — identify any terms used imprecisely and revise for accuracy
Analyse a published geographical description (e.g. from a geography journal, planning document) and identify how concept use and terminology contribute to its persuasiveness

response_modes.reason: Accurate and consistent use of geographical terminology requires practice and feedback. Students frequently use technical terms loosely. Consolidation through targeted vocabulary exercises and peer review of terminology precision builds reliable usage.

success_criteria: Produces a geographical description that uses at least three geographical terms accurately.
References at least one geographical concept explicitly in the description.

nodes.label: Geographical explanations supported by research findings
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct geographical explanations that use research findings (data, maps, statistics) to support ideas.
nodes.minimum_width: Students produce an explanation that uses at least two research findings as evidence and connects them to the geographical idea being explained.
nodes.typical_width: Students construct explanations using research findings to support ideas — e.g. data on water usage over time and at different places, or information about liveability indexes — ensuring that evidence is integrated into the explanation rather than listed separately.
wider: Construct an explanation using evidence from at least three different source types (quantitative data, map, qualitative interview/survey) and evaluate how the diversity of evidence types strengthens the explanation
Revise an explanation that makes claims without evidence — add appropriate research findings and evaluate how the revision changes the persuasiveness of the explanation
Analyse the role of maps as evidence in a geographical explanation — examine how spatial data is different from statistical data as an evidence type
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot integrate research findings into explanations produce claims-without-evidence, which fails the basic requirement of geographical communication. This is the skill that distinguishes geographical explanation from opinion, and it is required by all subsequent assessment tasks.

response_modes.reason: The move from presenting evidence and then making a claim (list-then-argue) to integrating evidence within an explanation (evidence-embedded argument) requires explicit practice. Consolidation through multiple explanation drafting and revision cycles builds this integration.

Practising evidence integration across both water and liveability content — and across different evidence types (maps, statistics, survey data) — prevents students from treating evidence integration as specific to one topic or data format.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Evidence-integrated explanation is the foundation of geographical communication and a transferable academic writing skill. Students who develop this across diverse content and evidence types have a robust writing toolkit applicable throughout secondary education.
success_criteria: Produces a geographical explanation that integrates at least two research findings as evidence within the explanation (not just appended).
Explains how each piece of evidence supports the geographical idea being argued.

nodes.label: Geographical representations as communication tools
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop geographical responses that use geographical methods — maps, data representations — to communicate conclusions and support arguments.
nodes.minimum_width: Students include at least one geographical representation (map, graph, data display) in a response and explain how it supports the argument being made.
nodes.typical_width: Students develop conclusions using geographical methods to represent data and information — e.g. a map showing water usage and scarcity in Australia, a map representing liveability indicators — integrating the representation into the response as evidence rather than decoration.
wider: Develop a response that uses multiple map types (distribution map, choropleth, flow map) for the same geographical topic and evaluate which best communicates the argument
Evaluate the communication effectiveness of a geographical representation (map or graph) and revise it to better serve the argument
Create a multi-modal geographical response (text + map + graph + photographs) and evaluate how the modes work together

response_modes.reason: Widening to multiple representation types and evaluating their fit for the argument being made builds understanding that geographical representation is a communication choice, not just a technical skill.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Selecting and integrating geographical representations as argument tools — not just as illustrations — is a sophisticated geographical communication skill. Students who develop this intentional approach to visual evidence have a significant advantage in geographical inquiry tasks.
success_criteria: Includes at least one geographical representation in a response and explains how it supports the argument.
Integrates the representation into the text of the response rather than presenting it as a separate appendix.

nodes.label: Integration: create complete geographical responses
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and responses that integrate geographical knowledge, methods, concepts, terminology and reference sources — producing coherent geographical communication.
nodes.minimum_width: Students produce a geographical response that includes description, explanation, at least one representation, and uses geographical terminology consistently.
nodes.typical_width: Students produce a complete geographical response — written, visual or multimodal — that integrates: accurate geographical description with terminology, explanation supported by research findings, at least one geographical method or representation, and references to sources — presenting the response as a coherent geographical communication.
wider: Produce a complete geographical inquiry report that integrates all elements across all sections — research question, evidence base, analysis, conclusion, strategy — as a professional quality geographical document
Evaluate a peer's geographical response against the four elements of the standard (description, explanation, methods, terminology) and provide structured feedback

response_modes.reason: The standard brings together description, explanation, representational methods and terminology into a single coherent response. Integration practises producing all elements as a unified geographical communication rather than assembling separate components.

success_criteria: Produces a geographical response that includes description, explanation supported by evidence, and at least one geographical representation.
Uses geographical terminology accurately and consistently throughout.
